analysis.one_liner: Puts crypto trading under a new, lighter-touch regulator and carves most tokens out of securities law.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 294-134 with 78 Democrats joining every voting Republican, but a Senate procedural vote to begin debate failed 49-50 in September 2026, leaving the bill stalled.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLARITY Act would build a new regulatory system for crypto. It defines most tokens as 'digital commodities' regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission instead of the Securities and Exchange Commission, lets token sales raise up to $50 million without securities registration, and excludes decentralized finance platforms from registration. It does add rules: exchanges, brokers, and dealers must register, keep customer assets separate, and follow anti-money-laundering law. A separate title bans the Federal Reserve from issuing a digital dollar.
analysis.who_benefits: Crypto companies above all. Token issuers gain an exemption from securities registration for sales up to $50 million a year and a path to being treated as commodities rather than securities. Exchanges and brokers gain legal certainty and a permanent, registered place in the financial system under a lighter regulator. Decentralized finance platforms are explicitly excluded from registration. Banks gain clear permission to hold crypto for customers. Retail investors also gain something real: registered platforms, segregated customer funds, and anti-fraud rules in a market that has largely operated without them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Crypto issuers, exchanges, and DeFi platforms

how_it_helps.text: Exchanges, brokers, and dealers must register with the CFTC, follow trade-monitoring and recordkeeping rules, and keep customer assets from being commingled with company funds.
Digital commodity platforms are brought under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring anti-money-laundering programs, customer identification, and suspicious-activity reporting.
Individuals are guaranteed the right to hold their own crypto in self-custodied wallets and transact peer-to-peer.
A short-title provision states that existing ethics rules bar members of Congress and senior executive branch officials from issuing a digital commodity while in office.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of tokens, mostly. Assets the bill classifies as digital commodities escape the SEC's full disclosure and registration regime — sales up to $50 million a year are exempt, and once a blockchain is 'mature' the token is treated as a commodity even if it was sold like an investment. Buyers lose securities-law protections and sue-for-fraud rights they would have under current law. The SEC gives up jurisdiction over most of the market, and the Federal Reserve is barred from issuing a central bank digital currency, foreclosing that option outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail token buyers, and the SEC's jurisdiction

drawbacks.text: Token sales of up to $50 million per issuer per 12-month period are exempt from securities registration, and a token is no longer treated as an investment contract once its blockchain is certified 'mature' — moving assets that behave like investments outside the disclosure and anti-fraud regime investors rely on.

Platforms in provisional registration may keep trading previously listed assets until joint rules take effect, and the CFTC may exempt registered firms from requirements to promote 'responsible innovation and fair competition.'
Decentralized finance trading protocols and messaging systems are expressly excluded from registration, leaving a growing corner of crypto trading outside the new licensing system.
The bill permanently prohibits the Federal Reserve from issuing or facilitating a central bank digital currency, eliminating that policy option rather than studying it.

Critics of moving crypto oversight to the CFTC point out that the SEC has a far larger investor-protection staff and enforcement record than the CFTC, which the bill tasks with policing a new market while also funding studies on fraud and foreign participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers something the current lawless market lacks: registered platforms, segregated customer funds, anti-money-laundering rules, and clear lines of authority. That is a real gain for the many ordinary people who hold crypto. But the design tilts the trade heavily toward industry: the same people who buy tokens are the ones who lose securities-law disclosure and fraud protections, the $50 million registration exemption is broad, the DeFi carve-out is large, and the CFTC is a thinner watchdog than the SEC. A bill written to protect token buyers first would look different — tighter limits on the exemption, fewer carve-outs, and more resources for the regulator taking on the market.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide bipartisan vote, but when the Senate tried to open debate in September 2026 the cloture vote — a motion needing 60 senators to cut off a filibuster — failed 49-50, one vote short, leaving the bill on the Senate calendar while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on July 17, 2025, 294-134, with 216 of 220 voting Republicans in favor and 78 of 212 voting Democrats in favor.

The Senate Banking Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on May 14, 2026, and it was reported by Senator Scott of South Carolina on June 1, 2026.
On September 15, 2026, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 49-50: 44 of 45 Senate Democrats and both Independents voted no, while 49 of 53 voting Republicans voted yes and 4 Republicans defected.
Senator Tillis entered a motion to reconsider the failed cloture vote the same day, leaving the door open to another attempt.
The bill would move most digital assets to the CFTC as 'digital commodities,' exempt qualifying sales from SEC registration, and ban Federal Reserve issuance of a central bank digital currency.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, crypto companies are the losers — the legal clarity they sought did not pass, and the market stays in its ambiguous state, with the SEC keeping the authority the bill would have taken away. Token buyers keep today's stronger securities-law protections for the time being, and the Senate Democrats who blocked the bill hold the leverage for any future deal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Token buyers' protections, and Senate Democrats' leverage

sides.party_line_note: In the House every voting Republican supported passage (216-0) while Democrats split 78-134; in the Senate the split was total — 0 of 47 Democrats and Independents voted for cloture versus 49 of 53 voting Republicans, with 4 Republican defections deciding the 49-50 outcome.

industries.note: The bill makes exchanges, brokers, and dealers registered CFTC intermediaries — locking in their role as the permanent gatekeepers of crypto trading — while imposing registration, segregation of customer assets, and anti-money-laundering duties. Legitimacy and obligation arrive together, but under a lighter-touch regulator than the SEC.

industries.industry: Token issuers and crypto project founders
industries.note: Issuers can raise up to $50 million per year without securities registration, and once a blockchain is certified 'mature' the token leaves securities law entirely. What issuers gain in freedom from disclosure is the disclosure regime token buyers lose.

DeFi trading protocols and messaging systems are expressly excluded from registration, leaving this corner of the market outside the new rules. Retail users trading there retain none of the protections registered platforms must offer.

The bill clarifies that banking institutions may hold digital assets in custody for customers and excludes bank custody activities from the new definitions. Banks gain a new line of business; customers gain the option of bank-held custody.

The SEC cedes jurisdiction over most digital assets to the CFTC, with anti-fraud authority only over a narrow set of transactions. Its mission — investor protection — is the same interest retail token buyers have in keeping securities rules.

The bill ties 'permitted payment stablecoin' to the GENIUS Act regime, integrating its framework with the already-enacted stablecoin law and excluding stablecoins from the commodity definition. Issuers gain a clear lane; payment users depend on the reserve standards in that separate law.

analysis.trajectory: The Senate has the bill on its calendar and a motion to reconsider the failed cloture vote is pending. With 49 committed Republicans, the bill needs roughly 11 more votes; that math requires significant concessions to Senate Democrats, who blocked it unanimously. Possible paths are a renegotiated version with stronger investor-protection terms, a late-session attempt during a must-pass legislative window, or the bill expiring at the end of the 119th Congress. Given the unified Democratic bloc against the current text, another attempt without changes would likely fail the same way.
